topic: Why the Moon shows us one face

opening.say: Look at the Moon on any clear night, and you'll notice it always shows the same familiar face.
So here's a puzzle. Does that mean the Moon never spins, or is something sneakier going on?
Hold that thought, because the answer depends on comparing two different clocks, one for spinning and one for circling Earth.

more.say: Picture yourself walking around a campfire while always facing it. Your friends watching from far away would see every side of you.
Now picture walking around that same fire with your back turned to nothing in particular, facing a distant tree the whole time instead.
Only one of those walks lets the fire see just your face. Keep that campfire in mind while we look at the Moon.

plan.setup: Watch the Moon as it circles Earth.
plan.narration: [[orbit-starts]]The Moon circles Earth once in about twenty-seven days. [[spin-matches]]And it spins once in that same time. [[face-locked]]So the same side always points at us. [[far-side]]The far side isn't dark, it's just hidden. [[tidal-origin]]Earth's gravity slowed the spin long ago.
plan.plan:
orbit-starts: Earth sits at center, and the Moon moves along a circular orbit around it, with one hemisphere shaded a different color.
spin-matches: A small arrow on the Moon rotates as it moves, completing exactly one full turn per full orbit, so the arrow's tip tracks the orbit.
face-locked: A line from Earth to the shaded hemisphere stays attached the whole way around, so the shaded side always faces Earth.
far-side: The unshaded hemisphere is highlighted facing away, lit by the Sun, to show it gets day and night too.
tidal-origin: Gentle bulges on the Moon point toward Earth while its spin slows until it locks to the orbit.
plan.close: If the Moon didn't spin at all, what would we see?
